lines.note: Fishing lines and ropes complete hikitakuru's winding sense from f194. The next sense begins arrebatar across this row and the next.

runs.text: batar, on tomar por força. Mas neſte ſegun-

lines.note: Seizing by force is the additional sense. On remains the printed-looking conjunction here, rather than being silently normalized; força has a faint but present r.

runs.text: do ſentido melhor ſe vſa, fittacuri, u.

lines.note: For the snatching sense the dictionary prefers hittakuru. This Japanese recommendation is printed within the italic explanation.
Hikitateru is raising someone by pulling them up. The next line specifies taking their arm.
Taking someone by the arm completes the literal action. Ware to begins a new Japanese example and its initial V is not part of the italic gloss.
Ware to kokoro o hikitatsuru means taking heart or encouraging oneself. Tç, not cç, supplies the historical tsuru ending.
Esforçar-se completes self-encouragement. Hito o hikitatsuru introduces promoting or supporting another person.
Helping someone by raising their standing continues the second example. Aleuantandoo is the historical u spelling of the lifting verb.
Giving a person status or position explains this figurative social advancement, not merely lifting their body.
Hikitaomeru is bending something downward by pulling. The damaged m was mistaken for n; the branch example supports taome.

runs.text: ou abaixar como ramo de aruore, &c.

lines.note: A branch of a tree illustrates the downward bending action, completing the previous definition.
Hikitsukuroi is arranging or dressing someone suitably. The conjugational endings ô and ôta have clear circumflexes in the scan, confirmed in the second pass.
The attendants are dressed more carefully than usual. Monodomo is the plural group word; mortodomo was an OCR error. The unusual Tomonǒ is retained with its visible mark.
Itsumo yori no hiki tsukurōte completes the preparation of those attendants. The Portuguese begins dressing and adorning them.

runs.text: atauiando aos que acompanhauão melhor que

lines.note: The accompanying people are dressed better than ever, matching the comparative expression rather than a new entry.
Nunca finishes melhor que nunca, the Portuguese comparative conclusion.
Hikitsumeru means drawing a bow fully or holding it taut. The beginning is damaged but the repeated example confirms hiki-, not hida-.
Yumi o hikitsumuru explicitly gives the bow as object; Idem refers to the same tautening sense.
Permet introduces the figurative kokoro o hikitsumeta hito, a person with a firm or concentrated mind. The terminal l introduces an alternative wording below.
Hikitsumeta hito is glossed as a resolute, tenacious person, extending the bow's tautness figuratively.
Em algũa couſa specifies what the person is tenacious about. It completes the metaphorical example.

runs.text: Cuſtume, ou ordem de fazer al-

lines.note: Hikitsuke is a written custom or order for doing something. This is a noun entry before the corresponding verb.

runs.text: gũa couſa que ſe deixa eſcrita pera ao diante

lines.note: The procedure is left in writing for future use, explaining its documentary character.
Future action should conform to that written instruction. Ella refers back to the recorded custom or order.
Hikitsukeru is drawing something toward oneself or making it approach. The example first concerns a boat.
An approaching vessel completes the literal illustration; Fi- begins a new example with hito.
Hito o hikitsukuru is presenting someone to another person. The old -kuru form is retained rather than modernized.

runs.text: ante doutro como pera o fazer ſeu conheci-

lines.note: The introduction is intended to make the person known to the other, continuing the Portuguese apresentar construction.
Do completes conhecido, ending the introduction example; it is not a Japanese particle.
Hikitsururu is taking someone along. The first inflectional letter is r, not i, as supported by the old verb ending.
Hikitsuru describes a contracted sinew. Encolhido, with l, explains contraction rather than the OCR encothido.

runs.text: neruo, &c. ¶ Item, Eſtar o veſtido en

lines.note: After the sinew example, the entry turns to clothing that has puckered. En- begins the following Portuguese adjective.

runs.text: gorruuinhado, & apunhado por eſtar mal coſi

lines.note: The clothing is gathered or puckered because of bad sewing. Preserve gorruuinhado and apunhado as printed; the second pass restores u in apunhado. Cosi continues into cosido on the following line.

runs.text: do ou mal alinhauado. ¶ Item, Puxar, ou leuar

lines.note: Bad stitching or basting causes that puckering. A further literal pulling sense begins after Item.
Puxando finishes carrying something by pulling, the last sense of hikitsuru here.
Hikitsutsumu is wrapping or covering. The final mi of the stem was misread as rri by OCR; ũda is nasal abbreviation in the past form.
Hikitodomaru is stopping or remaining, the intransitive counterpart to the next entry.
Hikitodomeru is restraining another person. Ter mão is the Portuguese expression for checking or holding someone back.
A alguem supplies the person restrained and closes the transitive definition.
Hikitomeru means stopping something by pulling it. The object follows in divided algũa.
The visibly irregular couſo is retained as printed-looking rather than automatically changed to couſa; its meaning remains the thing being stopped.

runs.text: Fiqitori, u, otta. i, Fittori, u.

lines.note: Hikitoru, with the alternative hittoru, is withdrawing an army. The nominal troop object follows below.
Ninju o hikitoru is withdrawing the personnel. Preserve the printed punctuation around the preceding exercito phrase.

runs.text: Recolher, ou retirar agente. ¶ Item reti-

lines.note: Recolher or retirar a gente translates troop withdrawal; the next reflexive retirar-se begins at the end.
Retirar-se and recolher-se extend the entry to withdrawing oneself. The long-s reflexive suffix is not j.
Hikitōsu is making something pass through by pulling. The inflectional u and oita are plain here, not ui and an accented initial o.
Hikyū denotes a little-known treatment point, as the next column explains through cauterization. The final marked u was entirely lost in the OCR headword.

runs.text: onde ſe dão botões de fogo que logo aproueitão

lines.note: The concealed point is where botões de fogo are applied. This is a historical treatment description, not a claim of present-day medical efficacy.
The dictionary says the application helps pain or illness. Fiqiù begins the Japanese suru example, preserving its local accent form.

runs.text: Dar botoẽs de fogo neſte lugar.

lines.note: Hikyū o suru means applying those cauteries at that spot. The Portuguese explicitly repeats the location.
Hikiwakareru is separation of two or more parties. The faint i after F is restored from the type and compound pattern.
Many people may likewise separate into the two sides, completing the reciprocal separation sense.
Hikiwakaru has the same meaning as the preceding verb; Idem deliberately avoids repeating the gloss.
Hikiwakeru is separating or dividing, transitive in contrast with the preceding paired intransitives.
Hikiwataru is passing or extending across something. The cloud example specifies the movement below.

runs.text: como nuuem, ou neuoa que paſſa por algum

lines.note: A cloud or mist passes over terrain, giving a spatial rather than interpersonal sense of wataru.
Monte completes the mountain example. This short row remains part of the cloud definition.

runs.text: Certo concerto de comer que ſe

lines.note: Hikiwatashi here is an arrangement of food, a noun separate from the following crossing verb.
Festivals or weddings are occasions for this food arrangement. Vodas is retained as the historical wedding spelling.
Hikiwatasu is making something pass across a place. The illustration leads a person over a river.
Hito no te o totte takes a person's hand. Totte has no extra r; ca- begins kawa in the next row.
Kawa o hikiwatasu means leading across the river. The damaged internal ta is recovered from context and traces rather than leaving an impossible split fiqiua aſu.

runs.text: mão fazello paſſar o rio. ¶ Item, atra-

lines.note: The person is made to cross while held by the hand. Item begins an additional sense of laying something across.

runs.text: ueſar, ou eſtender algũa taboa, pao, &c.

lines.note: A board or timber can be extended across something. Preserve the printed atravessar spelling instead of treating it as Japanese material.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Leuar em carretas pellas ruas a

lines.note: Another application is carrying a person through streets in a cart for public punishment; the purpose continues below.

runs.text: juſtiçar, ou por à vergonha, &c. Vt,

lines.note: Execution or exposure to shame explains that procession. Fi- starts the Japanese person-object example.
Hito o hikiwatasu repeats the procession sense. Kyō no begins a further example concerning a text or scripture.
Kyō no jimen o hikiwatasu concerns the literal written surface of a book. Jimen is not ground or land in this gloss.

runs.text: ou ſuperficial ſomente dalgum liuro, ou dar

lines.note: Only the literal or superficial meaning is explained; another option is a rapid reading of the book.
A quick look through the book completes that reading sense, linking watasu with passing across a text.
Hikiokoshi is also the name of a plant. The source gives no identifying botanical description here, so the note does not supply one.
The verb hikiokosu is waking and raising someone. The inflectional u is plain rather than grave-accented.

runs.text: tar ao que eſta dormindo. ¶ Item, Per-

lines.note: The person is asleep. Per- begins the editorial metaphor marker, not the next Japanese word.

runs.text: met. Tornar a aleuantar, ou renouar o que es-

lines.note: The figurative extension is reviving something forgotten or past; es- begins estava below.

runs.text: taua eſquecido, ou paſſado, como demanda,

lines.note: An old claim or dispute illustrates something revived. The Portuguese relative clause continues from the previous line.
Another literal sense is raising timber; a second heavy object appears in the continuation.
A large stone completes the list of objects lifted by hikiokosu.
Hikioru is breaking something by pulling. The full hiki- element distinguishes it from the OCR Fiquori.
Ki no yeda o hikioru is breaking a tree branch. Quebrar is one Portuguese word despite a weak interior impression.
Hikiorosu is lowering by pulling, with orosu providing the downward motion.
Hikiotosu is pulling something down or making it fall. This differs slightly from the controlled lowering gloss above.
The verb also means deducting in accounts, a figurative lowering of the amount.
Hikiukeru is receiving. Sake o begins an example of accepting a poured drink, not a palatalized hyuke lexical form despite the mechanical hint.
Sake o hikiukete nomu is receiving wine in a cup and drinking it. Ukete is the receiving verb within the compound.
Beber finishes the act of drinking from the preceding line.
Hikyūto denotes a very short person, with Issunbōshi offered as another expression. The alternative is Japanese within the italic explanation and the long vowels remain as printed.
Sed minus proprie qualifies that alternative as less exact. It is Latin editorial evaluation, not part of the Japanese noun.
Hikishirizoku is retreating or moving back. The past ending oita is legible despite its damaged initial vowel.
Moving backward completes the second Portuguese equivalent of retreat.
Hikishi(w)oru concerns pulling the bowstring. The printed xiuori spelling remains unchanged rather than normalized to a modern verb.
The purpose is drawing or readying the bow, completing the preceding string-pulling gloss.
Hikiyaburu is tearing or breaking. The scan has y rather than the OCR j, with the initial hiki restored from damaged print.
Hikiyoru is approaching, intransitive in contrast with the next drawing-near verb.
Hikiyoseru is drawing something toward oneself. Puxando continues on f196; the lower do. repeats that continuation as a catchword.
Catchword do. anticipates do. Vt, at the opening of f196 and completes the divided puxan-do across the page boundary. Its original stable ID is retained outside the body.
